subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Sensor Fusion
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Sensor Fusion.

hook.text: No single sensor is good enough on its own—cameras, lidar, and radar each have blind spots.

buildup.text: Cameras read color and text, lidar maps shapes in 3D, and radar tracks speed through weather.

discovery.text: Sensor fusion combines data from all of them into one coherent picture of the world.

twist.text: When sensors disagree, the fusion algorithm must decide which one to trust in milliseconds.

climax.text: Getting fusion right is what separates a car that stops safely from one that runs a red light.

punchline.text: Combining weak sensors creates one strong perception system.

quiz.question: What does sensor fusion do?
options: Merges data from multiple sensors into one view

details.summary: Sensor fusion combines data from cameras, lidar, radar, and ultrasonic sensors into a unified model of the vehicle's environment, where each sensor's strengths compensate for the others' weaknesses.
details.whyItMatters: No single sensor is reliable in all conditions. Fusing multiple sensor types creates a more robust and redundant perception system, which is essential for the safety of autonomous driving.
takeaways: Fusion combines cameras, lidar, radar, and ultrasonics
Each sensor compensates for the weaknesses of others
Disagreements between sensors create decision-making challenges

faq.question: What happens when sensors disagree about what they see?
faq.answer: The fusion algorithm must weigh confidence levels from each sensor and resolve conflicts. Typically, the system gives more weight to the sensor best suited to current conditions, like radar in fog or cameras in clear daylight.

faq.question: Is sensor fusion computationally expensive?
faq.answer: Yes. Processing and correlating data streams from multiple sensors in real time requires powerful onboard computers. The computing hardware in autonomous vehicles rivals that of small data centers.
